notes: Actual results for calendar year 2025, as the county reported them in its annual report to the Washington State Auditor. Not a budget.
Public schools are run by separate school districts, so they are not included.
Spending is reported by function (BARS account) for every fund, utilities included; capital expenditures count under their function when paid.

Internal service funds (equipment rental, self-insurance, information technology and the like; $1,787,716,000 of their revenue and spending) are left out, since the departments they serve report that spending.
Borrowing, transfers between funds, interfund loans, refunded debt and depreciation are left out.
General government, courts, legal services, planning, economic development, housing and conservation count as overhead.

Political money counts cash contributions from businesses, unions and PACs to county commissioner, council, executive, sheriff, prosecutor and other county office candidates, reported to the Public Disclosure Commission since 2023. Transparency practices have not been checked yet, so they are not scored.

Red flags: surveillance programs come from the EFF Atlas of Surveillance, a public database of news reports and public records, searched on 2026-10-18. A town or county with none listed may still have programs nobody has reported. Data center deals, corporate tax breaks and license-plate cameras mapped by volunteers have not been checked for Washington yet. Most records carry no dollar amount, so each documented program costs a quarter of the red-flag points instead of being counted as spending.

Debt outstanding: $4,926,879,000 (long-term plus short-term debt at the end of the fiscal year ending 2024-12-31), as King County reported it to the U.S. Census Bureau's 2024 Annual Survey of Local Government Finances. The state's own data does not report debt. That is a different year from the revenue and spending shown (FY 2025).

notes: Actual results for calendar year 2025, as the city reported them in its annual report to the Washington State Auditor. Not a budget.
Public schools are run by separate school districts, so they are not included. Residents also pay King County.
Spending is reported by function (BARS account) for every fund, utilities included; capital expenditures count under their function when paid.

Internal service funds (equipment rental, self-insurance, information technology and the like; $17,193,384 of their revenue and spending) are left out, since the departments they serve report that spending.
Borrowing, transfers between funds, interfund loans, refunded debt and depreciation are left out.
General government, courts, legal services, planning, economic development, housing and conservation count as overhead.

Political money counts cash contributions from businesses, unions and PACs to candidates for mayor and council, reported to the Public Disclosure Commission since 2023. Washington allows business and union contributions to local candidates. Individuals, candidates' own money, in-kind gifts, and party and caucus committees are not counted.
Transparency practices have not been checked yet, so they are not scored.

Cameras: 14 license-plate cameras are mapped inside City of Bellevue's borders in OpenStreetMap (9 made by Flock Safety), not counting cameras tagged as run by stores, malls, schools or state and regional agencies. Flock cameras count as a red flag whoever runs them. Other brands count only when the government is the recorded operator, since many have no operator recorded.

Red flags: surveillance programs come from the EFF Atlas of Surveillance, a public database of news reports and public records, searched on 2026-10-18. A town or county with none listed may still have programs nobody has reported. Data center deals and corporate tax breaks have not been checked for Washington yet. Most records carry no dollar amount, so each documented program costs a quarter of the red-flag points instead of being counted as spending.

Debt outstanding: $271,794,000 (long-term plus short-term debt at the end of the fiscal year ending 2024-12-31), as City of Bellevue reported it to the U.S. Census Bureau's 2024 Annual Survey of Local Government Finances. The state's own data does not report debt. That is a different year from the revenue and spending shown (FY 2025).

Who runs each camera is not recorded; cameras tagged as run by stores, malls, schools or state and regional agencies are not counted.
